**0.97h**

# Making progress on my Starbie!!

I'm completely new to hardware, electronics and all that jazz, so I found the best way to start was by reading the guide. It's quite helpful, but there are some parts that I find are kind of lacking, but Google generally helped anyways :)

It took me some time to get through navigating KiCad for the first time and getting through everything I need to download before I actually started on my schematic. Most of the language I find isn't that helpful, like, what in the world is a GND??? Though, I do applaud making me find out for myself by conducting my own research. ### 2026-10-06 – # footprints are nightmares

**1.15h**

# footprints are nightmares
Yeah that's an exaggeration but I really struggled with footprints today...

I'm a very visual learner, and I pretty much entirely relied on the images provided in the guide for creating the schematic. Of course, because the written instructions didn't provide exact details, I had to figure out how exactly what parts I needed and where to add them, such as whether or not I needed to use wires to connect all the pins to the microcontroller, though I eventually figured out net labels already do that. I suppose, however, that's the beauty of learning a new thing, isn't it? Below is an attached image of my hard work.

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 214725](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/d7134354fcc82c8623583c05491c4ee34ce91974df0bd6796edd7a5df19619dc.png)

This schematic is pretty much only based on the image I could see in the guide, which caused some problems because I forgot multiple items when assigning the footprints. The first issue was that I had no idea *HOW* to assign footprints, and had to use my elite visual understanding to identify that you had to use the search bar at the top to filter out specific footprints. It was at this time when I realized that I somehow forgot the resistor (though I quickly added it in) and didn't understand why my U1 and U2 were switched. Despite the schematic designing being only around half the entire guide, it took me far too long and too many questions to figure out. Eventually I had everything match the image **exactly**, though I can only imagine what problems can arise later down the line...

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 215709](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/2b991728d02753b57113c60b0ce86a3779845f7b27f15a06de6b62a58476cef5.png)

### 2026-10-08 – # Finally routed the PCB!

**1.7h**

# Finally routed the PCB!
I'm mostly done with the basics of the PCB now and all the technical stuff on it, but now I have to focus on the creative side of things. I've always been indecisive when it comes to "adding something personal" to a creation, and it took me far too long to figure out what I wanted to do.

After converting the schematic to the actual PCB design, the first thing I had to choose was what shape to make the PCB. Most people chose stars, which makes sense, but I wanted my own to have some flair to it. I watched countless videos of other people making similar projects, including one that explained how to use your own images as templates for the PCB. I also reviewed some of the other journal entries that people had for their Starbie. Ironically, I still went with a star, but I wanted mine to be even and symmetrical. It took a LOT of fiddling around trying to get my edges perfectly straight, and they're still a little wonky. Though, I'm happy where I am right now:

### 2026-10-09 – # routing errors and customization!

**1.88h**

# routing errors and customization!
The first part of my session was getting to fix all the errors that happened yesterday with my routing. Now, I thought I did a relatively good job, but apparently I had 20 errors when I went to check... Though, most were relatively mundane and easy to fix.

What I couldn't understand, however, was the GND pour. I knew I needed to route areas with the blue lines, yet I had several blue lines that weren't routed and didn't match the picture. Moreover, the picture had a huge red tint over it. I had no idea what a GND pour was, so I simply ignored it and told myself I would add it when I fixed the errors - but it was the thing causing the errors. It took me some time to figure out that a GND pour essentially connected all the parts with the net GND on them, which was exactly what I was missing:

![Screenshot 2026-10-08 224305](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/7142becc5f2b761c24e85afdd29d4bab13f3a8601d6a32a09a32664f632a1531.png)

I'm pretty proud of myself for figuring that out on my own! The second part of my session was getting all the customization of the board done before I moved on to the things inside the screen. I saw that the board in the guide had images and text on the PCB itself, but it never really explained how to get them. Though, I did want to figure it out on my own without relying on the guide the entire time. After at least 10 different Youtube videos, I finally figured out how to add images and text onto the PCB, but I wanted to have Pokemon sprites on it. What I couldn't understand was how KiCad converts the images into bitmaps that it can put onto the PCB, because sprites are notoriously small (only a few pixels across). As a result, when I put the sprite through the image converter, it came out looking almost blurry. Having to find and search for more images that were of higher quality on top of having to research how to even add images made up for the time in this session. It was all worth it and I think my PCB is coming together!

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 013406](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/11aa5648d9fac3e7daeac4e598aa5b7b0fabc021dd5438120fc40fb028f7efdd.png)

tl;dr is that I had to fix and figure out the routing errors of my PCB, and then research how to add images and text, though I had problems with the resolution of the images.

[Timelapse](https://lookout.hackclub.com/api/media/69da2acd-108a-4a45-bf44-b4464350bd1c/video.mp4)

### 2026-10-10 – # finishing up the customization!

**0.4h**

# finishing up the customization!

I've decided that I've spent far too long customizing and making lots of trial-and-error mistakes, so I spent this short session just making a final design. From what I've learned with my previous uploads of images, KiCad uses the image converter to make a bitmap and tries its best to match the original image using only 2 colours (this can be adjusted using the black and white threshold). It also has issues with extremely small images that it has to scale up. This was problematic for me because I wanted to have sprites on my PCB that are notoriously only a few pixels across. As a result, it smoothened out my image, which made it look completely wrong...

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 141938](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/e454924d51b9560478edd113033e7580e07f5fbaa78b206da44a081127768fbb.png)

So, learning from my mistakes, I decided to look for images that already have a clear black outline that is easy to differentiate from the light colours (i.e., no dark grey items as it is too similar to black). Eventually, I came up with this:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/a7a5b9103a4bcadf42ca3ab4f18a7607d7c6b4c6a7906decde7a4de19eeb5172.png)

tl;dr is I looked for large size, clear black outline images with contrasting colours so I can finish up the customization on my PCB

### 2026-10-10 – # started on firmware with lots of research!

**1.98h**

# started on firmware with lots of research!
After completely finishing my PCB, I'm now working on the firmware for the actual pet things. I started by downloading Arduino along with all the libraries that the guide requested, as well as seeing the code that was provided. The comments were especially helpful in figuring out what exactly I needed to do since it explained what the code did well. I'm not a beginner to tweaking values to make something my own, so I knew that the firmware was going to be my favourite part.

Before I started customizing, however, I noticed that it asked to "match your own wiring", or matching the XIAO label to the correct corresponding GPIO value. It said to change it only if my submission has a different layout, but I meticulously changed mine to match the guide exactly, so I thought this wouldn't be an issue. However, I discovered that my SDA values and my SCL values were swapped, with the SDA being put with the D5 label and vice versa. I had no idea if that mattered or not, but I double checked with the guide to see if they had the same swap, which it did. This took me to multiple websites (I recommend: https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/XIAO_ESP32C3_Getting_Started/ and https://randomnerdtutorials.com/esp32-pinout-reference-gpios/ to get a gist), though I still don't fully understand if this is something I should be worrying about.

*Edit: I asked about this on #half-life, and it's ust a small error in the guide and can be fixed later when I actually start building :)*

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/1734890111b52bea7f1e169fe34749bdb0297fe0b27b6fbbe4a34f9c7468c371.png)

(the SCL and SDA may have to be switched?)

For the customization part, I looked mostly at the code comments and what the guide said. At this point, I wanted to establish exactly what I was going to put on my Starbie so I didn't spend too much time thinking about it. My PCB already has a Jolteon on it, so I decided to make my creature a Jolteon, and change all the names of the actions to better fit the theme. Furthermore, I also wanted to change some of the graphics. At the end of the guide, it mentions making a sparkle trail and changing the pixel values to make your own shape, and I wanted to apply that to other items, such as replacing the hearts with lightning bolts. The guide didn't explain how drawing pixels works in Arudino, so I looked on the Adafruit GFX Graphics Library to get an understanding ( https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-gfx-graphics-library/graphics-primitives and
http://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-gfx-graphics-library?view=all)

Drawing a pixel essentially means deciding whether a pixel is on based on its relative position to an "anchor point". From this, I created:

display.drawPixel(x + 2, y, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x, y + 1, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x + 1, y + 1, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x, y + 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 1, y + 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 2, y + 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 3, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 2, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 1, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x + 1, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x + 2, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x + 3, y + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x, y + 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x + 1, y + 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x + 2, y + 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x, y + 5, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 1, y + 5, SSD1306_WHITE);
display.drawPixel(x - 2, y + 6, SSD1306_WHITE);

Which will hopefully create:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/e2c61a442ba5a81151fc07cea896fd49a0dbc984c468968cf9e5e2723c62843e.png)

To make this, I simply used Piskel, an app for creating sprites, to draw out what I wanted my lightning bolt to look like before I started drawing the pixels. I know that the guide also mentioned using another method to draw the actual creature, so I'll definitely be using Piskel for that since it gives a preview with monochromatic OLEDs.

tl;dr is that I worked on the firmware for Starbie, finding out that my SCL and SDA GPIO values were swapped, and discovering how to draw pixels in Arduino to create my own custom graphics on the OLED

### 2026-10-10 – # finding all the parts for the PCB...

**1.8h**

# finding all the parts for the PCB...

Up until this point, I was mostly going blind in on what exactly the parts of Starbie does. Obviously an OLED displays and the microcontroller runs the code, but all this was just basic information. As you can imagine, I had some trouble when compiling my BOM.

The microcontroller (XIAO ESP32C3) was relatively easy to find on Amazon, along with the OLED display, the motion sensor, and the temperature/humidity sensor (pretty self-explanatory what they do). It was at the point when I had to find the switches, resistor, and connector pins that I found out about DigiKey, which offers more reputable electronic parts (at least, compared to Amazon), and at a cheaper price. The shipping to Canada also isn't bad in terms of price and accessibility, which is a problem since most vendors prioritize the US. Additionally, vendors often sell switches, resistors, and small items in bulk, which can be frustrating when I really only have the Starbie project. Why would I purchase 100 resistors if I'm only going to use 1? Because DigiKey allows you to purchase just a few items, it was extremely helpful with the BOM. Eventually I also switched to purchasing the microcontroller on DigiKey, since it, surprisingly, offers a cheaper price compared to Amazon. However, DigiKey specializes in raw electronic components, hence why I decided to purchase the sensor and OLED on Amazon.

What took up most of the time was not only finding the exact product I needed, but also figuring out *what* product I needed. DigiKey offered hundreds of results for just searching up 10k resistor, each with different specifications. Did I need a through-hole or a surface mount resistor? Did I need a male pin, specialty pin, or female socket?? Why do they have GENDERS!? Looking at the 3D-viewer in KiCad helped immensely because I could actually visualize what a "through-hole" resistor meant, and compare it to what I saw on DigiKey. The pins were by far the most confusing, as neither the male pin or female socket looked correct to me based on the 3D-viewer, since it almost appeared flat? Though, I eventually figured out it was a male pin by looking at the underside of the PCB, since it actually showed the pin.

After a lot of confusion and research, I compiled my BOM by getting materials from both Amazon and DigiKey:

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 203834](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/287b245ebaf05de8ed2e1d2d562e6e5e0fd6dbece2a212330c4fece28313b5fc.png)

The total for this BOM was $37.54. However, I also purchased more than 1 of certain parts, because I know I have a tendency to accidentally break items especially when I only have 1 of them. If need be, I can reduce the amount, but I'll have to be extra careful... Because this is also just a chart, I included the manufacturer numbers, manufacturer, link, and other information for easy purchasing later :)

At this point I also decided to create a list of items that are not part of the PCB itself but are needed to assemble it, such as a soldering iron, solder wire,  a transfer cable, jumper wires, wire cutters, and a soldering tip cleaner.

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 203910](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/db8f7d840b8e3a48c982a4f095c10d647dd4f5461d91b0b025699c3074e238c2.png)

*EDIT: After looking at #half-life on Slack, I think I'm supposed to get Cherry MX switches, not the standard switches you see in electrical circuits, which are more expensive. The total is now ***$41.32 CAD, excluding taxes.**

tl;dr is that I found all the parts in the PCB and compiled them into a BOM, but it took lots of extra research because I had no idea exactly what specifications I needed for my part

### 2026-10-11 – # I messed up on the BOM but I fixed it!!

**1h**

# I messed up on the BOM but I fixed it!!

The guide actually has a BOM of its own, so I saw it and realized I was not only getting the wrong parts, but I was also spending way more than I actually should have. I was just buying in packs of 100, 10, or 50 for cheaper unit prices, but the BOM requires you to put in items as if you were buying the entire pack. I'm pretty sure the example BOM in the guide really isn't a good example, but after countless questions on #half-life with some of the reviewers I figure out:
* Your BOM on the Half Life website has to be under $30 to get the grant
* You can buy some items out of pocket
* Your BOM on your Github Repo has to include the original price of all items, assume no promotion/special discounts as they are not applicable to every person
* If you already own an item, you don't need to include it in your BOM (include it in the Repo BOM though)
* Your BOM should include taxes and shipping

After lots of research on several websites, including local stores for the better deals (compared to Amazon), I came up with the following BOM:

![BOM-AMAZON3](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/9da39e70cbe8f451db6f4556d7e13cf28d11dd0d402819343fcd6fe9c1c1ed7a.png)

![BOM-BCROBOTICS](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/4798c37b6664a77dc8210336ac0a29ee3e7b38f76d9468e2d9cf250005ca651c.png)

![BOM-JLCPCB](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/fdf6dc3a4f00416db964230d6aac0fa9ee3eef0f5b3ca122c25a07201aa57452.png)

![BOM-UNIVERSALSOLDER](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/00032edbb5eb72f45bb71bba2788e97faa0f23b85ce1f7634f39d84cf444e314.png)

This comes up to just under $26 USD, which fits in the budget! Shipping prices were definitely the most trouble for me, because some shipping prices were cheap but didn't get to me on time. I also added everything to my repo on Github to get ready to submit!

tl;dr is that I spent some time looking for products to add to my BOM after lots of talks on #half-life, coming out to just under $26 USD

### 2026-10-11 – # adding a switch

**1h**

# adding a switch

After being in a huddle on #half-life, I learned I should probably add a switch to add some more customization apart from just the art. To do this, I had to use one of the pins that is not already used on the ESP32, to which I chose D7. Then, I duplicated SW2 to make SW3, and then created the net label GPIO7 to connect both.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/0fef4043b36570ddb58477352637417028c84ecc2f0fd446ff705bf78ecc2d09.png)

So this is my final PCB, complete with an added keychain hole and extra switch! I had to update the cover image, video, and repo before I submit.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/604b7879bac46d49ea50f0bec69e013750b497434c59af601fa60e2e1d42c843.png)

I also edited some of the code in the Arduino to actually make the button do something, and I made it do the attack reaction automatically.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/ccccf5c7c09ac27a0691cb934dae778caf92b998386f08538902f008fd766b48.png)

tl;dr is that I added a new switch onto my PCB by editing both the schematic and layout, and then I made it do the Attack animation when pressed in Arduino
